newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP warns against tax rise to balance books.
newsitem.headline: German FDP warns against tax rise to balance books.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners, reiterated on Tuesday their opposition to raising taxes to plug a yawning budget gap.
"Tax increases...would destroy the budding economic recovery and lead to further unemployment," former economics minister Otto Lambsdorff of the FDP told German radio.

Pressure has been mounting in Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU) to raise fuel taxes or value-added tax after Bonn announced a tax revenue shortfall of 18 billion marks ($11 billion) last week.

But the FDP has staked its political survival on lower taxes and the party's opposition to tax hikes or a possible postponement to a cut in the solidarity tax -- levied to pay for the reconstruction of east Germany's economy -- limit Finance Minister Theo Waigel's options for balancing the books.

Lambsdorff said he understood why Waigel -- fighting to qualify Germany for European economic and monetary union (EMU) -- had not ruled out tax increases but said his position was not very helpful for relations in the ruling coalition.
FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told journalists in Bonn his party would only agree to an increase in indirect taxes if that was part of a wider tax reform including income tax reductions.

Gerhardt said his party, which Kohl needs to maintain his 12-seat parliamentary majority in the current parliament, was not planning to pass a formal motion against any kind of tax hike when it meets for its party congress this weekend.
But Walter Doering, the leader of the FDP southwestern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg, said he planned to introduce a motion calling on the party not to approve any rise in fuel tax.

The FDP also rejected a call from a senior CDU member of parliament, Friedhelm Ost, to cut the so-called "solidarity surcharge" on income tax by only one percentage point at the beginning of next year instead of two as planned.
"The FDP must say to itself...we want to avoid tax increases so we will forego one percentage point cut in the solidarity tax," said Ost, the chairman of parliament's budget committee.
The government plans to cut the special tax surcharge from 7.5 percent to 5.5 percent.
The FDP says the only way to solve Germany's current budget crisis is privatisation and deregulation.
"What we now need is a clear message for the reduction of the state's role through the cuts to taxes...and subsidies," FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms said in a statement.
Solms said he supported the earliest possible sale of the government's remaining stake in telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom which Waigel has mooted as one way to improve Bonn's cashflow.
